mainTopic: נקדימון's sun miracle, verses of curse read as blessings, and the reed versus the cedar
overview: This amud finishes the story of נקדימון בן גוריון. He had borrowed water for the עולי רגלים and promised to repay it by a deadline. His first prayer brings overflowing rain. The official then claims the sun had already set, so נקדימון prays again, and the sun breaks through the clouds; a ברייתא says this is how he got the name נקדימון. Next, a ברייתא lists three people for whom the sun broke through: משה, יהושע, and נקדימון, and the גמרא brings three sources for משה. The גמרא then returns to the משנה's case of a city with no rain, where רב teaches that both cities are cursed. רב יהודה follows with several harsh verses that he reads as hidden blessings, ending with the shaking reed, which is better than בלעם's cedar. A ברייתא teaches that a person should be soft like a reed, and a story about רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון begins; it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The official celebrates while נקדימון prays in sadness
steps.stepSummary: The הגמון mocks the idea that rain could still come and goes happily to the bathhouse. At the same time, נקדימון goes sadly to the בית המקדש to pray.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The official said:] 'And now it is going to rain?!' He went into the bathhouse happy. While the official happily went into the bathhouse, נקדימון went into the בית המקדש sad. He wrapped himself [in his טלית] and stood in prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: The story sets up a sharp contrast: the official is sure he has won the bet, and נקדימון turns to prayer. This scene prepares for the miracle that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The day is almost over and no rain has fallen, so the official expects to collect the silver. The text places the two men side by side on purpose. One trusts in the calendar and his contract, and the other trusts in תפילה.

keyTerms.meaning: A non-Jewish official or governor; here, the lender of the water
He wrapped himself (in a prayer shawl)

phrases.english: And now it is going to rain?!
phrases.notes: The official's mocking words. The day is nearly over.

phrases.english: He entered the bathhouse in joy.
phrases.notes: He expects to collect the silver.

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁהַהֶגְמוֹן נִכְנַס בְּשִׂמְחָתוֹ לְבֵית הַמֶּרְחָץ,
phrases.english: While the official entered the bathhouse in his joy,

phrases.aramaic: נַקְדִּימוֹן נִכְנַס לְבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ כְּשֶׁהוּא עָצוּב.
phrases.english: Nakdimon entered the Temple, sad.
He wrapped himself and stood in prayer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story begun on the previous amud
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The official celebrates his expected win while נקדימון turns to prayer.

steps.title: נקדימון's first prayer brings overflowing rain
steps.stepSummary: נקדימון tells הקדוש ברוך הוא that he acted only for Heaven's honor. Rain falls at once and overfills the twelve cisterns.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said before Him: 'Master of the World! It is revealed and known before You that I did not do this for my own honor, and not for the honor of my father's family. I did it for Your honor, so that water would be available for the pilgrims.' Immediately the sky filled with clouds, and rain fell until the twelve cisterns were filled with water and overflowed.
steps.whatsHappening: נקדימון prays, and his prayer is answered immediately with rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The core of his request is that his motive was pure. He wanted only to serve the עולי רגלים, not to win personal glory. The rain does not just fill the cisterns; it overflows, which shows the answer was generous.

keyTerms.meaning: Master of the World (a way of addressing God)
It is revealed and known before You
Pilgrims coming to ירושלים for the festivals
Became bound up or covered (with clouds)

steps.whyThisMatters: The prayer stresses doing a מצוה לשם שמים, for Heaven's sake. That pure motive is what makes him worthy of a miracle.

phrases.english: He said before Him: Master of the World!
It is revealed and known before You
that I did not act for my own honor,
and I did not act for the honor of my father's house,
rather, I acted for Your honor,
so that there would be water available for the pilgrims.
Immediately the sky became covered with clouds,
and rain fell

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁנִּתְמַלְּאוּ שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה מַעֲיָנוֹת מַיִם וְהוֹתִירוּ.
phrases.english: until the twelve cisterns were filled with water and overflowed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the content of the prayer begun in step 1 and its result
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A prayer made purely for Heaven's honor is answered immediately with abundant rain.

steps.title: נקדימון demands payment for the extra water
steps.stepSummary: The two men leave at the same time and meet. נקדימון tells the official to pay him for the extra water that overflowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the official came out of the bathhouse, נקדימון בן גוריון came out of the בית המקדש. When they met each other, he said to him: 'Give me the money for the extra water that you owe me!'
steps.whatsHappening: The two characters meet again, and נקדימון now turns the tables by asking the official for money. This sets up the official's counterclaim in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נקדימון did more than return the water. More water fell than he borrowed, so he argues the official now owes him for the surplus. The roles of debtor and creditor have flipped.

phrases.english: As the official left the bathhouse,

phrases.aramaic: נַקְדִּימוֹן בֶּן גּוּרְיוֹן יָצָא מִבֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ.
phrases.english: Nakdimon ben Guryon left the Temple.
When they met one another,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: תֵּן לִי דְּמֵי מַיִם יוֹתֵר
phrases.english: he said to him: Give me the money for the extra water
that you owe me!
phrases.notes: Literally: 'that I have in your hand.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the rain in step 2
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נקדימון claims the official now owes him for the surplus water.

steps.title: The official claims the deadline had already passed
steps.stepSummary: The official admits the rain came because of נקדימון. He still argues that the sun had already set, so the rain fell after the deadline and the silver belongs to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'I know that הקדוש ברוך הוא shook His world only for your sake. But I still have a claim against you that lets me take my money from you: the sun had already set, so the rain fell when it was already mine.'
steps.whatsHappening: The official challenges נקדימון with a technical argument: the payment deadline passed before the rain came.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not deny the miracle. He attacks the timing instead. The agreed day ended at sunset, and he says the rain came after that. By then the debt had already turned into a duty to pay silver, so the rain counts as falling 'on his property' and does not repay anything.

keyTerms.meaning: An opening of the mouth; a legal claim or argument
In my domain; under my ownership

steps.confusionAlert: The official is not denying that a miracle happened; he says so openly. His argument is only about timing: the rain came after the deadline.

phrases.english: He said to him: I know

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא הִרְעִישׁ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶת עוֹלָמוֹ
phrases.english: that the Holy One, Blessed be He, did not shake His world
except for your sake,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ לִי פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה עָלֶיךָ,
phrases.english: but I still have a claim against you,
by which I can take my money from you,
because the sun had already set,
and the rain fell in my possession.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ לִי פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה עָלֶיךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Counters נקדימון's demand from step 3
steps.kashyaTarget: נקדימון's claim that the rain repaid the debt and even left a surplus
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The deadline was sunset. The rain came after sunset, so the silver was already owed, and the rain cannot count as repayment.

steps.title: נקדימון's second prayer makes the sun shine again
steps.stepSummary: נקדימון returns to the בית המקדש and prays that הקדוש ברוך הוא show He has beloved ones in His world. The clouds scatter and the sun shines, so it is clear the day had not yet ended.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went back into the בית המקדש, wrapped himself, stood in prayer, and said before Him: 'Master of the World! Make it known that You have beloved ones in Your world!' Immediately the clouds scattered and the sun shone.
steps.whatsHappening: נקדימון answers the official's argument through a second prayer, and the sun comes out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The official's claim depended on the sun having set. The sun now shines, which shows it was still daytime. It had only looked like evening because of the heavy clouds. This time his request is to show the world how much הקדוש ברוך הוא loves His faithful ones.

phrases.english: He went back and entered the Temple,
wrapped himself, and stood in prayer,
and said before Him: Master of the World!
Make it known that You have beloved ones in Your world!
Immediately the clouds scattered
and the sun shone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Overturns the official's sunset argument from step 4
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sun had set, so the deadline had passed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sun was still in the sky; the day had not ended, so the rain came in time.

steps.title: The official concedes defeat
steps.stepSummary: The official admits that his claim would only have worked if the sun had not broken through.
steps.simpleTranslation: At that moment the official said to him: 'If the sun had not broken through, I would have had a claim against you to take my money from you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The official gives up his argument. This closes the main story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His words confirm that the miracle of the sun fully defeated his claim. The word נקדרה ('broke through') sets up the explanation of נקדימון's name in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: If (describing something that did not happen)

steps.whatToRemember: נקדימון's two prayers produced two miracles: rain to repay the water, and sunshine to prove the rain came before the deadline. Even the official admits it.

phrases.aramaic: בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה אָמַר לוֹ אוֹתוֹ הֶגְמוֹן:
phrases.english: At that time, that official said to him:
Had the sun not broken through,
I would have had a claim against you
by which I could take my money from you.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה אָמַר לוֹ אוֹתוֹ הֶגְמוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The official reacts to the miracle in step 5
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The miracle fully defeated the official's claim, and he admits it.

steps.title: A ברייתא explains the name נקדימון
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that his real name was בוני. He was called נקדימון because the sun broke through (נקדרה) for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: His name was not נקדימון; his name was בוני. Why was he called נקדימון? Because the sun broke through for his sake.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a ברייתא (a teaching from the time of the תנאים) that explains where נקדימון's name comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name נקדימון is read as coming from the word נקדרה, 'broke through.' His nickname became a lasting reminder of the miracle of the sun.

phrases.english: It was taught: Nakdimon was not his name,
rather, Buni was his name,
and why was he called Nakdimon?
Because the sun broke through for his sake.
phrases.notes: A wordplay: נקדימון comes from נקדרה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the word נקדרה used by the official in step 6
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name נקדימון comes from the miracle of the sun breaking through for him.

steps.title: Three people for whom the sun broke through
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the sun miraculously broke through for three people: משה, יהושע, and נקדימון בן גוריון.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: For three people the sun broke through for their sake: משה, יהושע, and נקדימון בן גוריון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that puts נקדימון in a list with two great leaders, משה and יהושע. In all three cases the sun broke through or stood still as a miracle for them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous step explained the name נקדימון from נִקְדְּרָה (broke through). This ברייתא uses a similar-sounding word, נִקְדְּמָה (came out early or broke through), to describe the same kind of sun miracle. That shared theme links this ברייתא to the story we just finished. The list sets up a question, because only some of these three cases have a clear source.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages taught. This opens a ברייתא, a teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה.
Broke through or came out early. Here it describes the sun shining in a miraculous way.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
For three people, the sun broke through for their sake:
Moshe, Yehoshua, and Nakdimon ben Guryon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the explanation of the name נקדימון (the sun נִקְדְּרָה, broke through, for him). It now places him in a list of three people who received this miracle.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sun miraculously broke through for three people: משה, יהושע, and נקדימון בן גוריון.

steps.title: We know the cases of נקדימון and יהושע, but where is the source for משה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא grants that נקדימון is known from tradition and יהושע from a verse. It then asks for the source that the sun broke through for משה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, we know about נקדימון בן גוריון from the tradition we just learned. We also know about יהושע from a verse: 'And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed.' But how do we know it happened for משה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks the sources for each name on the list. Two names are easy, but משה has no obvious verse, so the גמרא asks where it comes from. This question sets up the next three answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word בִּשְׁלָמָא (granted) means: these cases are fine. נקדימון comes from the story we just learned, and יהושע has a clear פסוק in ספר יהושע. The word אֶלָּא (but) marks the real question: no verse openly says the sun stood still for משה.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, or it makes sense. It accepts one part before asking about another part.
Here it means a received tradition, meaning the story just told. It does not mean the book of גמרא.
A verse from the Torah or the Prophets.
From where do we know this? It asks for a source.

steps.confusionAlert: Here the word גְּמָרָא does NOT mean 'the גמרא' we are learning. It means a received tradition, namely the story of נקדימון that was just told.

phrases.english: Granted, Nakdimon ben Guryon
is known by tradition (the story we just learned).
Yehoshua also has a verse,
as it is written: "And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, etc."
But Moshe, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the ברייתא by checking that each of its three names has a source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A scriptural source showing that the sun broke through or stood still for משה.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר learns it from the shared word 'I will begin'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר uses a גזירה שוה on the word אָחֵל, which appears both for משה and for יהושע. Whatever was done for יהושע was also done for משה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: We learn it from 'I will begin' and 'I will begin.' About משה it says, 'I will begin to put the dread of you.' About יהושע it says, 'I will begin to magnify you.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives the first answer. The same word, 'I will begin,' is used for משה and for יהושע, so we connect the two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse about יהושע continues: 'just as I was with משה, so I will be with you.' This shows that יהושע's greatness was modeled on משה's. The shared word אָחֵל ties the two together, so the sun miracle that happened for יהושע must also have happened for משה.

keyTerms.meaning: It comes from, or it is learned from. This usually introduces a גזירה שוה.
It is written here, and it is written there. This is the standard way to lay out a גזירה שוה.
To magnify you, or to make you great.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
It is learned from "I will begin" and "I will begin."
It is written here (about Moshe): "I will begin to put the dread of you,"
and it is written there (about Yehoshua): "I will begin to magnify you."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָתְיָא אָחֵל אָחֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question 'מנלן' about משה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה on the word אָחֵל links משה to יהושע. The miracle of the sun for יהושע therefore applies to משה too.

steps.title: רבי שמואל בר נחמני learns it from the shared word 'put'
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני uses a different גזירה שוה, on the word תֵּת. That word appears in the verse about משה and in the verse that introduces the sun standing still for יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said: We learn it from 'put' and 'put.' About משה it says, 'I will begin to put the dread of you.' About יהושע it says, 'On the day when ה' put the Amorites before Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a second answer to the same question. It uses a different shared word to link משה to יהושע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמואל בר נחמני chooses the word תֵּת because it appears in יהושע 10:12. That is the very verse where יהושע tells the sun to stand still. So his link goes straight to the sun miracle itself, not just to יהושע's general greatness.

keyTerms.meaning: On the day when ה' put the Amorites (before Israel). This is the day the sun stood still (יהושע 10:12).

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said:
It is learned from "put" and "put."
It is written here (about Moshe): "I will begin to put the dread of you,"

phrases.aramaic: וּכְתִיב הָתָם: ״בְּיוֹם תֵּת ה׳ אֶת הָאֱמֹרִי״.
phrases.english: and it is written there (about Yehoshua): "On the day when the Lord put the Amorites."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר אָתְיָא תֵּת תֵּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different source for the same answer as רבי אלעזר.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה on the word תֵּת links the משה verse directly to the verse about the sun standing still for יהושע.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן learns it from the משה verse itself
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן needs no גזירה שוה. The same verse about משה says the nations 'trembled and were in anguish.' That happened when the sun broke through for משה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: We learn it from the verse itself: 'who will hear the report of you, and tremble, and be in anguish because of you.' When did they tremble and feel anguish because of you? When the sun broke through for משה.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a third answer. רבי יוחנן finds the source inside the verse about משה, without comparing it to any verse about יהושע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says that all peoples 'under the whole heaven' would hear about משה and tremble. רבי יוחנן asks what event could make the whole world shake like that. His answer is a miracle in the sky that everyone could see: the sun breaking through for משה.

keyTerms.meaning: They trembled and were in anguish.

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא lists three people for whom the sun broke through: משה, יהושע, and נקדימון. נקדימון is known from tradition and יהושע from an explicit verse. For משה there are three sources: רבי אלעזר (a גזירה שוה on אָחֵל), רבי שמואל בר נחמני (a גזירה שוה on תֵּת), and רבי יוחנן (the משה verse itself, where the nations trembled).

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
It is learned from the verse itself:
"who will hear the report of you
and will tremble and be in anguish because of you."
When did they tremble and feel anguish because of you?
At the time when the sun broke through for Moshe.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר אָתְיָא מִגּוּפֵיהּ דִּקְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a third source. Unlike the first two answers, it does not depend on comparing to יהושע.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The nations' worldwide trembling described in דברים 2:25 must refer to a visible cosmic miracle: the sun breaking through for משה.

steps.title: Both cities in the rain verse are cursed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a city that got no rain. רב יהודה, in the name of רב, teaches that both cities are cursed: the dry one and the one that got rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And likewise a city that did not get rain, etc.' רב יהודה said in the name of רב: Both cities are under a curse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה's case of one city that gets no rain while the area around it does. רב יהודה says this is a curse for both cities, not just the dry one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse in עמוס sounds like only the dry city is punished and the other city is lucky. רב says the city that got rain is also cursed, because its rain comes as harsh, damaging storms. This flips the simple reading of the verse, and that sets up the next four teachings (steps 14 to 17), which flip harsh verses in the other direction.

keyTerms.meaning: רב יהודה said in the name of his teacher רב

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume the city that got rain is blessed. רב's point is that it is also cursed, because it gets too much rain and in a destructive way.

phrases.english: And likewise, a city upon which did not fall
rain, etc.
phrases.notes: 'Etc.' points to the rest of the משנה and the verse in עמוס 4:7.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
And both of them are for a curse.
phrases.notes: One city suffers drought. The other suffers damaging storms.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן עִיר שֶׁלֹּא יָרְדוּ עָלֶיהָ גְּשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This leaves the sun story from steps 8-12 and returns to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When rain falls on one city and not another, both cities are cursed: one by drought and one by harmful rain.

steps.title: ירושלים like a נדה is a hidden blessing
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, in the name of רב, reads the verse comparing ירושלים to a נדה as a blessing. A נדה becomes permitted again, so ירושלים will also be rebuilt.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'ירושלים among them was like a נדה.' רב יהודה said in the name of רב: This is for a blessing. She is like a נדה: just as a נדה has a time when she becomes permitted again, so too ירושלים has a repair.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching of רב יהודה that reverses the simple feel of a verse. Here a verse that sounds shameful is read as good news.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse in איכה compares ruined ירושלים to a נדה, which sounds like an insult. רב focuses on the fact that a נדה's separation is temporary and she returns to her husband. So the comparison itself promises that ירושלים's ruin will end.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman in her monthly period of impurity, separated from her husband

phrases.english: "Jerusalem among them was like a menstruating woman"
Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
It is for a blessing: like a menstruating woman.
Just as a menstruating woman has a time of becoming permitted,
so too Jerusalem has a repair.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is another teaching of רב יהודה in the name of רב that reverses a verse's simple tone. Step 13 found a curse where a blessing seemed to be. This step finds a blessing where a curse seems to be.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Comparing ירושלים to a נדה hints that her ruin is temporary and she will be restored.

steps.title: ירושלים only 'like' a widow
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה reads 'she has become like an אלמנה' as a blessing. She is only like a widow. She is really a wife whose husband went overseas and plans to come back.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'She has become like a widow.' רב יהודה said: This is for a blessing. 'Like a widow,' not an actual widow. Rather, she is like a woman whose husband went overseas and who intends to return to her.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives a second verse from איכה a hopeful reading. He builds it on the small word 'like.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse does not say ירושלים is a widow. It says she is like one. A real widow's husband is gone forever. A woman whose husband is far away only looks like a widow, and he plans to return. So the extra word 'like' teaches that הקדוש ברוך הוא has not abandoned ירושלים for good.

keyTerms.meaning: A country overseas, a faraway land

phrases.english: "She has become like a widow"
Rav Yehuda said: It is for a blessing.
Like a widow, and not an actual widow,
phrases.notes: The point rests on the letter כ, 'like.'

phrases.english: but rather like a woman whose husband went
to a country overseas,
and he intends to return to her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a second example of the same 'for a blessing' reading of a verse about ירושלים's destruction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Like a widow' means ירושלים is only temporarily without her Husband, who intends to return.

steps.title: Being 'lowly' spares us harsh government jobs
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה reads 'I have made you contemptible and lowly' as a blessing. Because the nations look down on us, they do not appoint us to harsh and hated official posts.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And I also have made you contemptible and lowly.' רב יהודה said: This is for a blessing. They do not appoint from us either river officials or government officers.
steps.whatsHappening: This is another of רב יהודה's hopeful readings. A verse in מלאכי that sounds like pure shame is shown to carry a hidden benefit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being looked down on by the nations seems only bad. But it also means they never draft Jews into burdensome and hated government roles, such as officials over rivers or enforcers of royal decrees. The disgrace itself protects us.

keyTerms.meaning: Government officers who enforce royal decrees

steps.whatToRemember: רב יהודה reads verses against their simple tone. The rain verse turns out to be a curse for both cities, while verses of shame (נדה, אלמנה, 'contemptible and lowly') each hide a blessing. The next step adds one more: the shaking reed.
steps.confusionAlert: 'For a blessing' does not mean the verse is not about punishment. רב יהודה agrees it describes suffering. He is showing a hidden hopeful side inside that suffering.

phrases.english: "And I also have made you
contemptible and lowly"
Rav Yehuda said: It is for a blessing,
for they do not appoint from among us
either river officials or government officers.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְגַם אֲנִי נָתַתִּי אֶתְכֶם נִבְזִים וּשְׁפָלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the third 'for a blessing' reading. It shifts from ירושלים to the Jewish people as a whole. A fourth reading, the shaking reed, follows in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Being lowly in the nations' eyes spares ישראל from being drafted into harsh official posts.

steps.title: The shaking reed is really a blessing
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, in the name of רב, says the verse 'ה׳ will strike ישראל like a reed shaking in the water' is meant as a blessing.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And ה׳ will strike ישראל as a reed shakes in the water.' רב יהודה said in the name of רב: this is for a blessing.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the fourth verse in רב יהודה's list of harsh-sounding verses that are really blessings. Here he says the image of a shaking reed is a good thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the surface, the verse sounds like a punishment: ישראל will be tossed around like a reed. רב יהודה says it is a blessing, but he does not yet explain why. The next steps give the reason.

keyTerms.meaning: A reed, a thin plant that grows by water

phrases.english: "And the Lord will strike Israel
as a reed shakes in the water" (I Kings 14:15)
phrases.notes: Said by the prophet אחיה השילוני

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
It is for a blessing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: לִבְרָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב יהודה's series of curses read as blessings (steps 14 to 16).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The verse comparing ישראל to a shaking reed is a blessing.

steps.title: אחיה's curse is better than בלעם's blessing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports רב יהודה with רבי יונתן's teaching: 'Faithful are the wounds of a friend.' The curse of אחיה השילוני is better than the blessing of בלעם הרשע.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: What does the verse 'Faithful are the wounds of a friend, and deceitful are the kisses of an enemy' mean? The curse that אחיה השילוני cursed ישראל with is better than the blessing that בלעם הרשע blessed them with.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for רב יהודה. A curse from a true friend, אחיה, is better than a blessing from an enemy, בלעם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse from משלי teaches that a friend's 'wounds' come from love and help you, while an enemy's 'kisses' are a trick. אחיה was a friend of ישראל, so even his curse holds a hidden good. בלעם was an enemy, so even his blessing hides harm. The next steps show exactly how.

keyTerms.meaning: אחיה from שילה, a prophet in the time of ירבעם
בלעם the wicked, the non-Jewish prophet who tried to curse ישראל

phrases.english: As Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"Faithful are the wounds of a friend
but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Proverbs 27:6)?
Better is the curse that
Achiya the Shiloni cursed Israel with
than the blessing that blessed them
Bilam the wicked.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source behind רב יהודה's claim in step 17.
steps.raayaObject: רב יהודה's claim that the reed verse is a blessing
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יונתן on 'Faithful are the wounds of a friend', comparing אחיה's curse with בלעם's blessing

steps.title: Why the reed is strong: it bends but stays
steps.stepSummary: אחיה compared ישראל to a reed. A reed grows by water, regrows when cut, and has many roots. Winds push it back and forth, but when they stop it is still standing in its place.
steps.simpleTranslation: אחיה השילוני cursed them with a reed. He said to ישראל: 'And ה׳ will strike ישראל as a reed shakes.' Just as this reed stands near water, its stump grows back, and its roots are many, and even if all the winds in the world come and blow at it they do not move it from its place, but it sways back and forth with them, and when the winds die down the reed is still standing in its place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why אחיה's 'curse' is really good. A reed bends with the wind instead of breaking, so it always survives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each detail of the reed is a hidden blessing for ישראל. It has water nearby, it grows back, and its roots hold it firm. Troubles may push ישראל around, but when the storm passes, ישראל is still standing.

keyTerms.meaning: Its stump grows back after being cut

phrases.english: Achiya the Shiloni cursed them with a reed;
he said to Israel:
"And the Lord will strike Israel
as a reed shakes."

phrases.aramaic: מָה קָנֶה זֶה עוֹמֵד בִּמְקוֹם מַיִם,
phrases.english: Just as this reed stands in a place of water,
and its stump grows back, and its roots are many,
and even if all the winds in the world
come and blow at it,
they do not move it from its place;
rather, it sways back and forth with them.
When the winds die down,
the reed stands in its place.
phrases.notes: So too ישראל will survive every hardship.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first half of רבי יונתן's comparison: the hidden good in אחיה's curse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The reed survives every wind by bending, so the 'curse' promises that ישראל will always survive.

steps.title: Why the cedar is weak: stiff until one wind topples it
steps.stepSummary: בלעם blessed ישראל by comparing them to a cedar. A cedar is not near water, does not regrow, and has few roots. Most winds cannot move it, but the south wind tears it out and knocks it flat.
steps.simpleTranslation: But בלעם הרשע blessed them with a cedar, as it says: 'Like cedars by the water.' Just as this cedar does not stand near water, its stump does not grow back, and its roots are not many, and even if all the winds in the world blow at it they do not move it from its place, but once the south wind blows at it, it uproots it and turns it on its face.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now shows the hidden harm in בלעם's 'blessing.' A cedar looks strong, but it cannot bend, so one strong wind destroys it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every detail is the opposite of the reed. The reed bends and survives; the cedar stays stiff and breaks all at once. בלעם's nice-sounding words secretly wished ישראל a sudden downfall.

keyTerms.meaning: A cedar tree, tall and stiff
The south wind, a very strong wind
Turns it over on its face, knocks it flat

steps.confusionAlert: The verse says 'cedars by the water,' but the גמרא says a cedar does NOT grow near water. That is the point: בלעם's words sound nice, but the real cedar lacks these blessings.

phrases.english: But Bilam the wicked blessed them with a cedar,
as it is said: "Like cedars by the water" (Numbers 24:6).

phrases.aramaic: מָה אֶרֶז זֶה אֵינוֹ עוֹמֵד בִּמְקוֹם מַיִם,
phrases.english: Just as this cedar does not stand in a place of water,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין גִּזְעוֹ מַחְלִיף, וְאֵין שׇׁרָשָׁיו מְרוּבִּין.
phrases.english: and its stump does not grow back, and its roots are not many.

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ כׇּל הָרוּחוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם נוֹשְׁבוֹת בּוֹ —
phrases.english: Even if all the winds in the world blow at it,
they do not move it from its place.
But once the south wind blows at it,
it uproots it and turns it over on its face.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the contrasting half of the comparison: the hidden harm in בלעם's blessing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The cedar's stiffness means one strong wind destroys it, so בלעם's 'blessing' secretly wished ישראל a sudden fall.

steps.title: Extra point: the reed becomes the pen for the Torah
steps.stepSummary: On top of that, the reed earned the honor of being made into a quill used to write ספר תורה, נביאים, and כתובים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And not only that, but the reed earned that a quill is taken from it to write with it a ספר תורה, נביאים, and כתובים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more advantage of the reed over the cedar. The reed is used to make the pen that writes holy books.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This goes beyond survival. The humble, bending reed is the one chosen to write the תורה. This finishes the proof that אחיה's 'curse' is better than בלעם's 'blessing.'

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but also
The Prophets and the Writings, the rest of תנ״ך

steps.whatToRemember: A curse from a friend (אחיה, the reed) is better than a blessing from an enemy (בלעם, the cedar). The reed bends and survives, and it even writes the תורה.

phrases.english: And not only that, but the reed merited
that a quill be taken from it

phrases.aramaic: לִכְתּוֹב בּוֹ סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה נְבִיאִים וּכְתוּבִים.
phrases.english: to write with it a Torah scroll, the Prophets, and the Writings.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a final advantage of the reed, closing the comparison.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The reed is honored to become the pen for writing holy books.

steps.title: Be soft like a reed, not stiff like a cedar
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches a life lesson: a person should always be soft and flexible like a reed, not hard and stiff like a cedar.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: A person should always be soft like a reed and should not be hard like a cedar.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that turns the reed and cedar into a lesson about how to act. Be gentle and flexible, not proud and rigid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps were about the fate of ישראל as a nation. Now the same picture becomes personal advice on character. Being 'soft' means being humble and easy to get along with.
steps.whyThisMatters: This line sets up the story that follows, which shows what happens when a great scholar acts 'hard like a cedar.'

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A person should always be soft like a reed
and should not be hard like a cedar.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: לְעוֹלָם יְהֵא אָדָם רַךְ כְּקָנֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the reed/cedar picture and applies it to personal character.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should always be humble and flexible like a reed, not proud and rigid like a cedar.

steps.title: Story begins: רבי אלעזר rides home feeling proud
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a story. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון was riding his donkey home from his teacher's house along the river. He was very happy, and he felt proud because he had learned a lot of תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an incident where רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון was coming from מגדל גדור, from his teacher's house. He was riding on a donkey and traveling along the riverbank, and he was very happy. And he was feeling proud because he had learned much תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story that illustrates the ברייתא. This is only the setup; the main event comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key detail is that his 'mind was thick upon him,' meaning he felt proud. That is acting like the stiff cedar. The story will show what goes wrong because of this.

keyTerms.meaning: A story, an incident that happened
From his teacher's house (where he learned)
He felt proud, full of himself

phrases.aramaic: מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁבָּא רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן
phrases.english: There was an incident where Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon came
from Migdal Gedor, from his teacher's house,
and he was riding on a donkey
and traveling along the bank of a river,
and he was very happy.
And he was feeling proud
because he had learned much Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁבָּא רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a story that illustrates the ברייתא about being soft like a reed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup of the story: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון was feeling proud of his תורה learning.
